title: Extract and count like a senior
summary: rg -o, grep -oE and the sort | uniq -c | sort -rn pipeline for incidents, lines versus matches, and the same counting in C# with Regex.Matches and LINQ.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: pull values out of logs and count them
steps.body: During an incident the first question is usually "which one, and how many?": which status, which client, which endpoint. These commands answer it in seconds, straight from the log.

toolkit.what: Print only the part of each line that matched, one match per output line. Several matches on one line give several output lines.
flags: only the matched text, not the whole line
no file names when searching many files
print a replacement instead of the match
toolkit.when: turning a log into a list of values you can count, sort or diff

toolkit.what: The same with grep, which is on every server and container. -E is needed for {3} and + without backslashes.
toolkit.when: on a box over SSH, or on the output of kubectl logs

toolkit.cmd: rg -oN 'status=[0-9]{3}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
toolkit.what: The classic count of distinct values, biggest first. uniq only merges lines that are next to each other, which is why the first sort is needed.
flags: put equal lines next to each other
one line per distinct value, prefixed with its count
toolkit.example: grep -oE 'ip=[0-9.]+' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 5
toolkit.when: which client, endpoint or error dominates right now

toolkit.what: Count matching lines, per file. It counts lines, not matches: a line with two ERRORs counts once.
flags: number of matches, even several per line
rg counts matches instead of lines
toolkit.when: a quick "how bad is it" number for the incident channel

toolkit.what: PowerShell, with .NET regex. Without -AllMatches it keeps only the first match on each line. Group-Object plays the part of uniq -c.
flags: every match on a line, not just the first
toolkit.when: on Windows servers and build agents

steps.prompt: Match each piece of the toolkit to what it does.
pairs: collapse equal neighbouring lines and count them
count every match, even several on one line
make Select-String keep every match on a line

steps.prompt: Complete the pipeline: list every HTTP status in the access log with how often it occurs, most common first.
steps.explain: `sort` groups equal lines, `uniq -c` counts each group, `sort -rn` puts the biggest count first. Plain `sort -n` would put the most common last. Keep the `-n`: it compares the counts as numbers, which stays right even when a count is wider than the padding `uniq -c` adds.

buckets: Rank distinct values: `... | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn`
items: How many requests failed, when each failure is one log line?
How many lines of the build log contain `warning`?
How many `TODO` markers are there, when one line can hold several?
How many IP addresses appear in total, several per line?
Which client IP sends the most requests?
steps.explain: `-c` counts lines. When a line can hold several matches, print each with `-o` and count those. When the question is "which", count each distinct value.

steps.prompt: On the same log, `grep -c 'ERROR' app.log` prints `3` and `grep -o 'ERROR' app.log | wc -l` prints `5`. Why?
options: `-c` counts matching lines, and some lines contain ERROR more than once
`-c` stops counting after the first match in each file
steps.explain: Three lines contain ERROR; between them they hold five. Say which number you mean when you post it in the incident channel.

steps.title: The same pipeline in C#
body: `Regex.Matches` returns a `MatchCollection`, which you can loop over or query with LINQ. `GroupBy` is `uniq -c`, and
int errors = Regex.Count(log, @"ERROR");        // .NET 7+: counts matches without building them
`Matches` is lazy: it finds matches as you read them, so `Regex.Matches(log, p).First()` does not scan the whole log.
When you only need the number, `Regex.Count` is cheaper: it never creates `Match` objects.

steps.explain: Four three-digit statuses, three of them after `GET`. `Regex.Match` returns the first match only: `404` comes before `500`.

steps.title: Every server error
prompt: You are about to run `rg -oN '<pattern>' access.log | sort | uniq -c`. Write the pattern that finds every 5xx
status, written as `status=` and three digits starting with 5. Include the `status=` part, so ids like `id=500` are

all.input:
GET /a status=200 dur=12ms
GET /b status=503 dur=30012ms
POST /c status=500 dur=8ms
GET /d status=404 dur=3ms

hints: A literal `status=5`, then two more digits.
steps.explain: Anchoring the number to its label is what keeps `id=500` and durations out of the count.

steps.title: Slow requests
prompt: Find every duration of one second or more: `dur=` followed by **four or more** digits and `ms`.

all.input:
GET /a status=200 dur=12ms
GET /b status=503 dur=30012ms
POST /c status=500 dur=8ms

steps.explain: Counting digits is a cheap stand-in for a numeric comparison. It works because the numbers have no leading zeros; for a threshold like 1500 ms, extract the number and compare it in code.

steps.title: uniq -c in C#
prompt: Write `List<string> CountStatuses(string log)`, the C# version of
- Find every `status=` followed by three digits with `Regex.Matches`.
- The code is the part after `status=`: `m.Value[7..]`.
- Return one string per distinct code, `"<count> <code>"`, most common first; equal counts by code, ascending.
For a log with three 500s, two 200s and one 404 the result is `["3 500", "2 200", "1 404"]`.
template:
var dojoLog = "GET /a status=200 dur=12ms
GET /b status=500 dur=30012ms
GET /c status=404 dur=3ms
POST /d status=500 dur=8ms
GET /orders/12345 status=200 dur=5ms
GET /e status=500 dur=40ms";
Dojo.Eq("three 500s, two 200s, one 404", new List<string> { "3 500", "2 200", "1 404" }, CountStatuses(dojoLog));
Dojo.Eq("equal counts sort by code", new List<string> { "1 200", "1 404" }, CountStatuses("status=404 status=200"));
Dojo.Eq("an empty log gives an empty list", new List<string>(), CountStatuses(""));
